Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time).
All participants were fluent in German, and 205 spoke German as their sole mother tongue.
Participants were recruited through newspaper and radio features, flyers, and social media channels.
Participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
All but four participants requested the feedback.

After preparations, participants were left alone and received all instructions via computer screen.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time).
All participants were fluent in German, and 205 spoke German as their sole mother tongue.
Participants were recruited through newspaper and radio features, flyers, and social media channels.
Participants provided written informed consent prior to participation.
All but four participants requested the feedback.
Participants were required to sign an informed consent form at the beginning of the first 156 session.
Participants were seated in a dimly lit, sound-attenuated, and electrically shielded recording cabin.
After preparations, participants were left alone and received all instructions via computer screen.

Participants completed a cued task-switching task (approx. 25 minutes) 39, a Posner letter matching task (approx. 15 minutes) 40, a Sternberg memory scanning task (approx. 30 minutes) 41, 42, and a simple two-choice reaction time task (approx. 10 minutes) 11, 43 .
After the second task, participants were offered snacks and drinks.
Each participant had the opportunity to ask questions and to see the study doctor before the MRI scan.
Upon arrival, participants completed an additional MRI eligibility screening questionnaire to ensure that their eligibility had not changed since the structured interview.
After undergoing a metal check to ensure they were not carrying any metal objects on their body or in their pockets, participants were positioned and prepared for the measurement in the scanner.
If resting-state data was acquired, participants filled in the German version of the Amsterdam Resting-State Questionnaire 2.0 (ARSQ) 44 outside the scanner after the last measurement was completed.
The operation-related component scores for each participant are calculated by aggregating the normalized z-scores of all tasks measuring the respective component.
Participants completed a battery of three binding tasks in a fixed order: letter-color, word-number, and location-letter.
In the letter-color binding task, each trial sequentially presented a short list of letter-color pairs that participants were asked to remember.
Participants were only instructed to respond as accurately as possible, but not to respond as fast as possible.
In the word-number binding task, participants completed two practice trials and 14 experimental trials, in which they were asked to remember pairs of nouns and two-digit 3.
In the location-letter binding task, participants were presented two practice trials and 14 experimental trials, in which they had to remember the location of a lowercase letter within a 3 x 3 grid.
Participants were instructed to either click on the letter belonging to the grid position indicated by the '?' or to click on the grid position belonging to the letter probed below the grid.
In contrast to the other two binding tasks, participants were neither instructed to answer as fast nor as accurately as possible.
To assess handedness, participants filled out the ten-item German version of the Edinburgh Inventory 34 .

Additionally, participants were asked to indicate in a single item whether they were left-or right-handed, with the option of selecting both (ambidextrous). in an alternating order throughout the session.
Participants were instructed to sit quietly in a comfortable position throughout the entire recording.
Before moving on to the next task, the participants were instructed to open their eyes.
During each trial, participants had to classify the target according to one of two task-sets.

Specifically, participants had to decide whether the target, a number between 1 and 9 (except 5), was either smaller or larger than 5 (task-set magnitude, orange) or whether it was odd or even (task-set parity, violet).
Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible, by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard.
Participants completed a version of the Posner task 40 .
Within our study, participants had to decide whether the two stimuli were semantically the same, independent of physical identity (i.e., upper or lower case).
Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard.
Participants completed a version of the Sternberg memory scanning task 41, 42 .

Trial conditions and presented numbers were randomized with the restriction that no probe occurred twice in a row, no more than three matching or non-matching trials occurred in a row, and the position of the probe in the number sequence could not be the same three times in a row.
In this task participants were asked to focus on a fixation cross that was flanked by a square on each side.
Participants had to indicate with a button press on which side the target appeared.
Trials were randomized, with the restriction that the presentation sides did not repeat more than three times in a row.

A subset of n = 163 participants completed an MRI-adapted parity/magnitude cued task-switching paradigm in the MRI machine while we acquired multi-band multi-echo blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signal data.
In each trial, the participants had to judge a single-digit number between 1 and 9 (excluding the number 5) according to one of two given task-sets.
In the parity task-set (violet), participants were asked to indicate whether the probe stimulus was an odd or an even number.
In the magnitude task-set (orange), participants were asked to indicate whether the probe stimulus was smaller or greater than 5.

Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible, by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard ("1" with the index finger for even/larger and "2" with the middle finger for odd/smaller).
Participants were instructed to fixate a white fixation cross on a dark gray background, to move as little as possible, and to let their mind wander without thinking of anything specific.

After the last MRI measurement and after the participants had left the scanning room, they checked their answers on a sheet of paper on a 5-point Likert scale ('Completely disagree' (--) to 'Completely agree' (++)).
Additionally, this file contains information on the order in which participants completed the three sessions and any issues that arose during the MRI session.
If participants completed the task-switching task in the MRI machine, the individual starting times and durations of all experimental blocks are saved in the *_events.tsv file in the func subfolder.
If participants completed a resting-state fMRI measurement, they filled in the ARSQ 2.0 after the last measurement and after they left the MRI scanner room.
The time limits for this participant were 11.9 s for the operation span, 16.5 s for the reading span, and 26.5 s for the symmetry span.
These participants had accuracies < 55%, suggesting they might not have adhered fully to the task instructions.
Furthermore, for the ARSQ 2.0 one participant had more than 75 % missing responses.

However, the data from the cued task-switching task should not be used or used with caution for four participants who did not adhere to the task instructions or had overall low accuracies as described in Section Quality control of behavioral recordings.
Participants were shown how head and body movements can result in EEG artifacts.
Thereafter, participants were instructed to find a comfortable sitting position and move as little as possible during the tasks.
Furthermore, participants were instructed to focus on the center of the screen, as all tasks would be presented in a centered manner.
Moreover, participants were instructed not to suppress blinks and to maintain their natural blinking pattern.
Participants were positioned in the MRI machine using cushions to stabilize the head within the head coil and to minimize head motion.
In addition, all participants were instructed to move as little as possible during the measurement.
Participants completed the operation span, the reading span, and the symmetry span task, with the order of the tasks being the same for each participant.
In the operation span task, participants were presented with three to seven processing tasks, each followed by a letter that had to be retained in the correct order of their presentation.
Participants were instructed to click on the previously presented letters in the correct serial order.
Participants had to judge whether the presented number was the correct solution for the math problem or not.
The reading span task was similar in structure to the operation span task but participants had to judge whether a given sentence was semantically meaningful or not as the processing task.
In the symmetry span task, participants were presented with two to five geometric figures that they had to judge as either symmetrical or not as a processing task.
After each geometrical figure, a highlighted screen position in a 4 x 4 matrix was presented that participants were instructed to store.
Participants were asked to correctly select the missing element from eight alternatives in order to complete the figure.

text.text: The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability.
The multi-indicator design supports latent-variable modeling of all major constructs alongside their structural, functional, and electrophysiological neural correlates.

Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time).
Electroencephalography (EEG) data was collected during four resting-state blocks and during task performance (cognitive control and processing speed).

High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging using the SANDI protocol, and multi-band multi-echo functional MRI during rest and task-switching were acquired in a subset.
Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data are accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository.
All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.

General cognitive ability is a defining trait of human cognition and yet, biological substrates as well as neurocognitive processes that potentially explain differences in general cognitive ability across individuals remain debated.
We define general cognitive ability following pertinent theories 1, 2 as a latent, hierarchical construct.
text.formatted: We define general cognitive ability following pertinent theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> as a latent, hierarchical construct.

text.text: The latent factor of general cognitive ability is reflected in a series of cognitive abilities, which in turn can be measured using cognitive tasks and tests such as memory tasks, reasoning and problem-solving tests, processing speed tasks, and verbal comprehension tasks, among others.
A latent general factor can explain the observation of the positive manifold: An individual's scores on different cognitive tasks tend to be positively associated.

Next to its pertinence in basic research, general cognitive ability has predictive value for many important life outcomes such as job performance and educational attainment 3, 4 , socioeconomic success 5 , and even higher life expectancy 6 , emphasizing the relevance of understanding interindividual differences in cognitive ability.

text.text: One previously hypothesized feature underlying cognitive ability differences is the speed of information processing 7 .

text.text: Research investigating behavioral (e.g., raw reaction times or model parameters of mathematical models of reaction times such as the diffusion model) or neural measures (e.g., the latency of components in the event-related potential, ERP) has consistently found that higher cognitive ability is related with faster behavioral and neural processing speed [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] .

text.text: Phrased differently, individuals with higher cognitive ability process information faster than individuals with lower cognitive ability.

While these findings may suggest that higher neural processing speed favors higher behavioral processing speed, which in turn leads to higher cognitive ability, empirical data do not support this assumption of a causal cascade.
Instead, research found that only a small part of the relationship between neural processing speed and general cognitive ability is mediated by behavioral processing speed 13 .

text.text: Likewise, an experimental increase of behavioral processing speed via nicotine administration did not increase performance on an intelligence test, as would be expected if a causal cascade model were true 14.

text.text: The neurocognitive process model 15 offers an alternative explanation to the causal cascade assumption.

text.text: The model suggests that properties of structural and functional connectivity of brain regions associated with higher cognitive functioning serves as a common underlying cause favoring both, a higher neural and behavioral processing speed and higher general cognitive ability.

This is supported by previous research investigating the fractional anisotropy as a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) derived marker for structural connectivity of the brain or generally the integrity of the white matter [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] [24] .

text.text: The neurocognitive process model proposes a relationship between cognitive ability and the integrity of the white matter such that individuals with higher cognitive ability benefit from a higher integrity of fronto-parietal tracts underlying higher cognitive functions such as working memory and cognitive control processes.

The model suggests that structural connectivity, in turn, favors higher functional connectivity of networks underlying these processes, allowing for more efficient working memory and higher cognitive control processes necessary to solve reasoning test items efficiently 24 .

text.text: Thus, the model assumes that the effect of structural connectivity on cognitive ability test performance is fully mediated through processing speed and working memory capacity and their neural correlates, reflected in ERP latencies and behavioral processing speed.
While the neurocognitive process model motivated the selection of constructs and measures in the present study, the dataset is not tied to a single theoretical account.
Competing frameworks make partially overlapping but distinguishable predictions about the neurocognitive architecture of cognitive ability.

text.text: The breadth of behavioral and electrophysiological measures in this dataset allows researchers to adjudicate among these accounts, or to combine them, rather than privileging any one.
Here, we describe a dataset from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years.

It includes comprehensive cognitive ability and working memory capacity assessments, task-based (cued-task-switching and different choice reaction time tasks) and resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) measures as well as structural (T1-, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted) and functional (task-based and resting-state) MRI measures.
Behavioral data -such as reaction times and accuracy -are available for all tasks.
The dataset was acquired as part of the Mainz Network Study, conducted between February 2024 and February 2025.

We chose the tasks and measures included in this dataset to cover the constructs cognitive ability, working memory capacity, behavioral and neural processing speed, and structural and functional connectivity of the brain, and to allow latent modeling of all constructs relevant to test the hypotheses of the neurocognitive process model 15.

text.text: Previously, cognitive ability test data and diffusion-weighted data of the Mainz Network Study were used in a study that derived and characterized measurement models for several white matter microstructure markers and assessed their relationship with fluid intelligence 28 .

text.text: Additionally, cognitive ability test data, binding and complex span task data, and behavioral and neural data acquired during the choice reaction time tasks were used in a study that tested whether the association between processing speed and cognitive ability is mediated by working memory capacity 29 .

text.text: Future research can benefit from the diversity of constructs measured and methodologies employed that will enable researchers to explore questions across various cognitive domains, such as working memory, cognitive control, or cognitive ability, as well as across different levels of resolution, from behavioral outcomes to underlying neural substrates in a healthy population.

What distinguishes the present dataset from other large-scale, openly accessible neuroimaging datasets, such as the Human Connectome Project (HCP) 30 , the MPI-Leipzig Mind-Brain-Body dataset (LEMON) 31 , the Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) 32 , and the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience project (CamCAN) 33 , is the combination of task-based EEG recordings obtained during a series of elementary cognitive tasks, multiband multi-echo functional MRI acquisition sequences, and state-of-the-art diffusion-weighted imaging based on the Soma and Neurite Density Imaging (SANDI) scheme.
text.formatted: What distinguishes the present dataset from other large-scale, openly accessible neuroimaging datasets, such as the Human Connectome Project (HCP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> , the MPI-Leipzig Mind-Brain-Body dataset (LEMON) <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> , the Amsterdam Open MRI Collection (AOMIC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> , and the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience project (CamCAN) <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> , is the combination of task-based EEG recordings obtained during a series of elementary cognitive tasks, multiband multi-echo functional MRI acquisition sequences, and state-of-the-art diffusion-weighted imaging based on the Soma and Neurite Density Imaging (SANDI) scheme.

text.text: Furthermore, although some of the aforementioned datasets also include measures of general or fluid intelligence obtained through standardized tests, the present dataset is unique in combining these measures with task-based EEG recordings and anatomical and functional MRI data acquired both at rest and during task performance.

text.text: The binding tasks are a set of working memory tasks constructed based on the binding hypothesis of working memory capacity 45 .
text.formatted: The binding tasks are a set of working memory tasks constructed based on the binding hypothesis of working memory capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> .

text.text: The binding hypothesis states that working memory relies on building, maintaining, and updating arbitrary bindings.
It assumes that interferences between bindings cause limited working memory capacity.
We programmed the binding tasks following the description in Wilhelm et al. 45 .
text.formatted: We programmed the binding tasks following the description in Wilhelm et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> .

text.text: Participants completed a battery of three binding tasks in a fixed order: letter-color, word-number, and location-letter.
In the letter-color binding task, each trial sequentially presented a short list of letter-color pairs that participants were asked to remember.
The task consisted of two practice trials with feedback on the correctness of participants' responses and 15 experimental trials without feedback.
At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross was presented for 1000 to 1500 ms.
Directly after, two to six pairs of a capital letter and a color-filled square were presented in the center of the screen.
The letter was always presented on the left side while the color-filled square was always presented on the right side of the screen.
Each pair was shown for 1000 ms followed by an inter-stimulus-interval (ISI) of 1000 to 1600 ms.
The beginning of each recall test was indicated by a '?' presented for 1800 to 2200 ms.
All previously presented pairs from that trial were probed in a random order with 50 % of probe stimuli being a color and 50 % of probe stimuli being a letter.
The probe stimulus (e.g. a color) was presented centrally on the screen with all possible pairing stimuli presented in a circle around the probe (e.g. all letters used in the respective trial).
No new stimuli were introduced; every pairing item had already been presented earlier in the trial.
Participants used the mouse to click on the correct answer.
Participants were only instructed to respond as accurately as possible, but not to respond as fast as possible.
After the mouse click (or after 30 s if no answer option was selected), the '?' appeared for another 1800 to 2200 ms followed by the next probe stimulus.
Across all the given answers of all participants, this led to four missing answers.
Trials were separated by an inter-trial-interval (ITI) of 3000 to 3500 ms.
All durations were randomly drawn from a uniform distribution.

text.text: In the location-letter binding task, participants were presented two practice trials and 14 experimental trials, in which they had to remember the location of a lowercase letter within a 3 x 3 grid.
After the presentation of a fixation cross for 1000 ms, two to six letters appeared sequentially in different fields of the grid.
Letters were presented for 1500 ms followed by an ISI of 500 ms.
The beginning of the recall phase was indicated by the German word 'Abfrage!' (English: 'Test!') presented on the screen for 1000 ms.
In 50 % of recall tests, the grid appeared with a '?' in one of the previously shown locations and the possible letters used in that respective trial appeared lined up horizontally below the grid.
In the other 50 % of recall tests, an empty grid appeared with a single letter below the grid.
Participants were instructed to either click on the letter belonging to the grid position indicated by the '?' or to click on the grid position belonging to the letter probed below the grid.
In contrast to the other two binding tasks, participants were neither instructed to answer as fast nor as accurately as possible.
Due to an technical error no maximum reaction time of 30 s was imposed.
Instead, the experimental code allowed for a maximum reaction time of 1000 s, which resulted in only one missing response across all participants.
Additionally, three responses exceeded 30 s, but all remained below 50 s.

text.text: This task required participants to switch between two categorization tasks.
During each trial, participants had to classify the target according to one of two task-sets.
The color of the fixation cross served as the cue indicating which task-set to use.

Specifically, participants had to decide whether the target, a number between 1 and 9 (except 5), was either smaller or larger than 5 (task-set magnitude, orange) or whether it was odd or even (task-set parity, violet).
The cue was always valid, such that cue and target had the same color throughout all trials.
A trial consisted of a sequence of four slides.
First the cue was presented for 400 to 600 ms.
The cue was followed by a blank screen (ISI) for 400 to 600 ms.
Then the target was presented until the participant responded, but always for a minimum of 1000 ms and a maximum of 3000 ms.
Lastly, there was an ITI of 1000 to 1500 ms, showing again a blank screen.
Presentation times were randomly selected from a uniform distribution.
The duration of one trial therefore varied between 2800 and 5700 ms, depending on cue presentation time, ISI and ITI, as well as participants' reaction time (i.e., target presentation time).
Participants spent on average 22 minutes on this task.
A total of 384 trials were presented.
Of all trials, 50 % were switch trials, requiring a shift in the task-set, and 50 % were repeat trials, requiring the same task-set as in the trial before.
Half of all trials belonged to each task-set.
Condition (switch vs. repeat) and task-set (parity vs. magnitude) were fully crossed.
Numbers were drawn at random with the restriction that neither task-set nor condition occurred more than three times in a row.

Mapping of response keys ("d" for odd/smaller and "l" for even/larger) was kept constant across participants.

text.text: In this task, participants have to judge whether a probe stimulus did or did not appear in a sequence of five numbers.

Within each trial, first a fixation cross was presented for 1000 to 1500 ms.
Then, a sequence of five numbers was shown (each 1000 ms), interspersed by a blank screen (ISI, 400 to 1000 ms).
After the last blank screen, the retention interval began (a slide with a centered question mark) and lasted for 1800 to 2200 ms.
The probe digit was presented subsequently until the participant responded, but always for a minimum of 1000 ms and a maximum of 3000 ms.
Lastly, a blank screen was presented for 1000 to 1500 ms (ITI).
Temporal jittering of presentation times was drawn at random from a uniform distribution.
Each trial endured between 11.8 and 18.2 seconds, depending on presentation times and participants reaction time.
On average participants spent 24 minutes on the Sternberg memory scanning task.

text.text: For the duration of the anatomical imaging, participants viewed a short movie with nature scenes for relaxation via a mirror that was attached to the head coil.
They were instructed to move the head and body as little as possible.

A subset of n = 163 participants completed an MRI-adapted parity/magnitude cued task-switching paradigm in the MRI machine while we acquired multi-band multi-echo blood oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signal data.
The subset resulted from the limited scanning time of one hour per participant, as the MRI-adapted task and corresponding task-state BOLD data were collected only when time permitted.
The task began at the onset of functional image acquisition (first scanner trigger), followed by an 8 s baseline interval and 12 blocks of 14 trials, totaling 168 trials.
Each block lasted for approximately 39.2 s, followed by an off-period of 20.8 s.
In each trial, the participants had to judge a single-digit number between 1 and 9 (excluding the number 5) according to one of two given task-sets.
Which of the two task-sets had to be applied was indicated by a colored fixation cross that appeared for 400 ms before the probe stimulus.
In the parity task-set (violet), participants were asked to indicate whether the probe stimulus was an odd or an even number.
In the magnitude task-set (orange), participants were asked to indicate whether the probe stimulus was smaller or greater than 5.
After an ISI of 400 ms, the probe stimulus appeared for 1500 ms.
There was an ITI of 500 ms before the next trial started.
Due to small delays caused by the screen's refresh rate, the timings per participant varied minimally.

Three of the task blocks were pure parity task-set blocks, three of the blocks were pure magnitude task-set blocks, and six blocks were switching blocks, in which one half of trials belonged to the parity and the other half of trials to the magnitude task-set.

In addition, 50 % of trials in the switching blocks were repeat trials (previous trial belonged to the same task-set) while the other 50 % were switching trials (previous trial belonged to the other task-set).
As in the cued task-switching task during the EEG measurement, numbers were drawn at random with the restriction that neither task-set nor condition occurred more than three times in a row.
Participants indicated their answers via a button box using the index and middle finger of the right hand.
They were instructed to press the index finger whenever the probe stimulus was even or larger than 5 and the middle finger whenever the probe stimulus was odd or smaller than 5.
Participants underwent a short training with performance feedback outside the scanner to familiarize themselves with the adapted version of the task.
The practice consisted of 10 trials for each task-set followed by 4 blocks of 14 trials each, mirroring the block design participants underwent in the MRI machine.

Participants were instructed to respond as fast and accurately as possible, by pressing one of two keys on the keyboard ("1" with the index finger for even/larger and "2" with the middle finger for odd/smaller).
If participants did not respond within 1500 ms of target onset, the trial was marked as missing and during practice, participants received the feedback "too slow".
Slides were dark gray (#808080) with either orange (#d95f02) or violet (#7570b3) stimuli, depending on the task-set.
This color set makes the task accessible for people with colorblindness.
Numbers and letters were presented in typeface Arial and font size 80.
All stimuli were centered horizontally and vertically.

The subset resulted due to the limited measurement time of one hour per participant.

Participants were instructed to fixate a white fixation cross on a dark gray background, to move as little as possible, and to let their mind wander without thinking of anything specific.

The BIS was conducted by one of three trained experimenters.
Before receiving formal training, each experimenter first participated in a session led by an experienced experimenter.
Subsequently, each experimenter assisted in at least one session, and later led at least one session under the experienced experimenter's supervision.
Because the training always included the entire behavioral session, all experimenters were familiar with the instructions for every task.
Similarly, experimenters were trained and practiced the procedure for the EEG and MRI sessions.
Experimenters responded to participants' questions, ensuring that the wording remained as similar as possible to that of the standardized task instructions.
Questionnaire and experimental data were directly and automatically collected via computerized experimental tasks.
Only the BIS and the ARSQ 2.0, being paper-and-pencil tests, required a manual evaluation.
The manual evaluation of the BIS was conducted by two trained, independent raters in accordance with the test manual.
All tasks related to the operation-specific components processing capacity, processing speed, and memory were scored by one rater using scoring templates.
A second independent rater performed random spot checks.
If the error rate exceeded 2 %, a complete second evaluation was conducted by the independent rater.
Any remaining discrepancies were resolved by an experienced researcher who supervised the manual evaluation.
All tasks related to the creativity component were fully double-rated.
Any remaining discrepancies were again resolved by an experienced researcher.
The participants.tsv file reports any issues that occurred during the sessions and that might be relevant for data analysis.
In particular, the data of sub-027 from the complex span tasks is not shared, as the participant did not adhere to the task instructions.

The time limits for this participant were 11.9 s for the operation span, 16.5 s for the reading span, and 26.5 s for the symmetry span.
None of the other participants reported such a strategy, but there are participants with equally high time limits.

EEG was recorded in a dimly-lit, electrically shielded, sound-attenuated recording cabin.

Before starting the recording, it was ensured that the impedance values of electrodes were sufficiently low and as uniform as possible.

Furthermore, participants were instructed to focus on the center of the screen, as all tasks would be presented in a centered manner.
Moreover, participants were instructed not to suppress blinks and to maintain their natural blinking pattern.
In order to guarantee optimal data quality, the preparation of electrodes, impedance checks, and visual data inspection were overseen by an experienced experimenter.

text.text: The complex span tasks are a set of working memory tasks that require participants to store information and recall it in the correct order at a later stage 47 .
text.formatted: The complex span tasks are a set of working memory tasks that require participants to store information and recall it in the correct order at a later stage <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> .

text.text: Between storage and recall, participants perform an intervening processing task.
In this study, we used the German version of three complex span tasks 46 .
text.formatted: In this study, we used the German version of three complex span tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> .

text.text: Participants completed the operation span, the reading span, and the symmetry span task, with the order of the tasks being the same for each participant.
In the operation span task, participants were presented with three to seven processing tasks, each followed by a letter that had to be retained in the correct order of their presentation.
The letters were presented for 800 ms each.
The recall test comprised of a 4 x 3 matrix containing all possible letters.
Participants were instructed to click on the previously presented letters in the correct serial order.
There was the possibility to click on a 'blank' button whenever the participant could not recall one letter at a certain position.
Participants could also clear all the letters they had already entered to correct their entries.
In the operation span task, the processing task consisted of math problems followed by a number (e.g., '(7 × 3) -3 =?' followed by '18').
Participants had to judge whether the presented number was the correct solution for the math problem or not.
There were 15 trials in total.
The reading span task was similar in structure to the operation span task but participants had to judge whether a given sentence was semantically meaningful or not as the processing task.
Again, three to seven processing tasks each followed by a letter were presented per trial and there were 15 trials in total.
In the symmetry span task, participants were presented with two to five geometric figures that they had to judge as either symmetrical or not as a processing task.
After each geometrical figure, a highlighted screen position in a 4 x 4 matrix was presented that participants were instructed to store.
In the recall test, participants saw an empty 4 x 4 matrix and were asked to click the previously highlighted screen positions in the correct serial order.
There were 12 trials in total.
All three complex span tasks were preceded by three blocks of practice trials.

In the first block participants practiced only the storage component (remembering and recalling a letter or a highlighted screen position in the correct serial position) in two trials with set size 2 and two trials with set size 3.
